-## #2987 - The first traverse of a 3+2 plane is judged against the machine table
-
-- **What was decided** (taken unattended; the maintainer can change it):
-  1. **The table's top face, not its slab.** In a 3+2 frame, the law reads the machine table as its top face over the stated X/Y travel (the table box clipped to the Z travel, which starts at the table top). The slab under it (`MAX_FIXTURE_DIM` deep) is out of the tool's reach. Along an axis that tilts past 90 deg, the slab's underside read about 5e5 mm; the top face reads the real height. The table box already has the X/Y travel as its footprint (`fixture::table_of`), so "clip to the travel" needs only the Z clip.
-  2. **Read the table only when the head tilts.** The machine file states which rotaries turn the work (`AxisLimits::turns_part`, #804). When each tilting rotary (axis not vertical) turns the work, the pose comes from turning the part. The tool stays upright in the machine frame, and the table stays under the work, so the stock top is the higher top. The index-swing clause (#1107) judges the work against the table in that case. The law then does not read the table. When a tilting rotary can be in the head (a head rotary, or an old file that does not state `turns_part`), or when the machine has no tilting rotary, the law reads the table top face along the tool axis. This is the conservative reading.
-  3. **The tool starts at the tool-change height, and the table counts only where the move along the tool axis from there can carry the tool under its top** (premise (b), chosen by the maintainer on 2026-11-20). The control does not know the tool's X/Y after a tool change, but the tool stands at the top of the Z travel (the table top plus the Z stroke, `GenJob::z_stroke`). The upright law has the same premise: it judges only the descent onto the plane. The worst start is any point of the X/Y travel at that height. The move along the axis from a start at local height `h` to the plane changes the world Z by `(plane - h) * axis_z`. When the axis points up (`axis_z > 0`), the table counts if that move can end more than `Z_TOL` under the table top. The verdict then names the lowest plane that every such move clears: `h_max - stroke / axis_z` along the axis, where `h_max` is the highest start reading. The in-plane traverse then runs between two points over the table top (a convex half-space), so it cannot go under it. A horizontal axis (B 90) never changes the Z and never counts the table, although the far X edge reads high along it. When the axis points down toward the table (past 90 deg, `axis_z < 0`), a higher plane stands lower in the world, and the verdict can only say "raise", which is wrong there. If the move can end under the table top, the path gets the note "...: the tool axis points down toward the table, so the move along it from the tool-change height (the Z travel top) to the clearance plane can go under the table top" instead of a verdict. A machine that states no finite Z stroke is read with stroke 0: a start on the table top, the stricter reading.
-     - Found by the stack gate: a B 90 pocket on `tilthead.mch` at clearance Z95 was refused "under the fixture top Z625", and the `multiaxis/indexed` catalog case "under the fixture top at Z500" (Front and Back pockets) and "at Z134.808" (Tilted pocket, A30 B30). With a start on the table top (premise (a)) the Tilted pocket's move ends 62.0 mm under the table top at the X+ Y- travel corner. From the tool-change height Z500 it ends at Z-124.5, 375.5 mm over the table top. The shipped catalog case does not change.
-     - **NOT covered:** a program that starts with the tool low near the table, for example after a manual jog. The operator must send the machine to its tool-change height before the program starts, as for the upright law.
-     - Dropped: premise (a), a start anywhere on or over the table top. It refuses the shipped catalog case for a start that a tool change never leaves (the tip parked on the table 1 m from the part).
-     - Dropped: drop the table from every 3+2 reading (the #2985 law). A plane that a move from the tool-change height takes under the table passes again (the wide-machine B 30 pin fails).
-     - Dropped: a new `Warning` that says "lower the clearance plane" for an axis that points down. It changes the verdict type in `sim`, `app`, `ui` and the MCP surface. Follow-up #3081.
-     - Dropped: refuse each plane past 90 deg with the "raise" verdict. Its height to clear is wrong for such an axis, and a refusal with a wrong repair misleads.
-  4. **No stated travel gives a note.** A mounted machine that does not state all of its X, Y and Z travel gives no table box (`fixture::table_of` needs the three). On a 3+2 plane that the table would judge, the path gets the note "First traverse: the machine table is not judged on this tilted plane: the machine does not state all of the X, Y and Z travel, so the first traverse is judged against the stock and the fixtures only". With no machine mounted there is no table, and no note (the unstated-limit law).
-- **Why.** The #2985 law skipped the table in each 3+2 frame. A head-tilt plane drops toward the table on its low side, so a collision with the table passed. A plain read of the full table box refused each indexed operation on the microARC 4 (`first_4axis_part`, `fourth_axis_pose`, `index_swing`, `tilt_a180`, `tilt_a180_routes`). Even the top face alone refused them (Z 190.5 at A 90, Z 336.55 at A 180). Those refusals are false: that machine turns the work, and its table never stands over the plane.
-- **Considered and dropped.**
-  - Read the table in every frame, clipped: refuses each shipped 4th-axis example (false refusals, Done-when item 2 fails).
-  - Read the table in the machine frame of a work-turning rotary: this needs the rotary axis line for an indexed operation. `fixture::rotary_axis_of` gives it only for the rotary kinds. No gain, because the table is under the work there.
-  - Refuse when the machine states no travel: each 3+2 operation on a vendor file without travel would stop posting. A note is visible and does not stop a legal program.
-  - A new `Warning` text for the table ("under the table top"): it changes the verdict type and the MCP surface. The existing "fixture top" text names the height to clear, which is the repair.
-- **Not judged (known).** The law runs at generation only (as in #2985). Loading a different machine after a generate does not judge the first traverse again until the next generate. A machine with a head tilt and a vertical work C is read without the C turn of the footprint. A mixed machine, with a work-turning tilt (for example a table A) and a head tilt (for example a head B), reads the table top face in the setup frame: the part turn of the work-turning tilt is not in that reading.
-- **Cost to change later**: low. One predicate (`work_tilts`), one clip (`table_top_face`) and one reading (`table_read`) in `operation/first_traverse.rs`.

-## #2996 - Widen verdicts only for models limited by the file tolerance
-
-The maintainer decided on 2026-11-20 to accept a true-surface bound up to
-0.030 mm for a model made coarse by the file's stated tolerance. The
-program header must state that bound. A model made coarse by the facet
-budget keeps the strict law of #864.
-
-### The rule
-
-A model's chord error `c` bounds the deviation of its kept mesh from the
-true surface. The importer promises `PROMISED_CHORD` = 0.005 mm. The
-excess is `e = c - 0.005`. Each gouge law holds a tolerance `t` and judges
-against the mesh at `t'`.
-
-The persisted `file_tolerance` record permits widening only when the file
-tolerance required the coarse mesh and the facet budget did not coarsen
-it further. Missing records, budget coarsening and mixed causes keep the
-strict law. A selection can widen only when every reduced source has the
-permitted cause. Import, project save/load, copies and undo preserve the
-record. Update undo restores each copy's own record, including a cause
-that differs from the source. This prevents one eligible part from
-widening another part.
-
-For an eligible model:
-
-| Chord `c` | Mesh tolerance `t'` | True-surface bound for `t = DEV_TOL` |
-|---|---|---|
-| up to 0.005 mm | `t` | at most 0.015 mm |
-| 0.005 to 0.010 mm | `t - e` (#864) | 0.015 mm |
-| over 0.010 to 0.020 mm (`WIDE_CHORD_LIMIT`) | `min(t - 0.005, 0.005)` | `c + 0.005`, at most 0.025 mm |
-| over 0.020 mm | `t - e` (#864) | no allowance at `DEV_TOL`: refused by name |
-
-An ineligible model uses `t - e` at every reduced chord. At `c = 0.012`
-mm, `DEV_TOL = 0.010` mm gives a mesh tolerance of 0.003 mm. At or above
-`c = 0.015` mm, that law has no tolerance left and refuses the operation.

-  smaller deduction made by the widened mesh law.

-     - Work and turning steel stand at the C angle the post states before X and Z move, so they are read exactly: each facet (a box as its twelve facets) is clipped by each band's planes. -     - Fixed steel (a tailstock, the machine table) stands in the machine frame at an angle the part frame does not state. It is read revolved about the spindle: its nearest and farthest radius against each band, and its top against the band's floor. That holds at any C.

-**Cause.** Cargo 1.100 puts each workspace unit in its own directory,
-`target/<profile>/build/<package>/<hash>/` (rlib or test exe, pdb,
-fingerprint). The hash covers the unit's profile. Read in the shared build
-worktree `issue-917` on 2026-11-21:
-
-- The manifests, `Cargo.lock` and `.cargo/config.toml` were the same at
-  the last six heads that were gated there.
-- The `profile` hash in the fingerprint of the same test unit
-  (`world_init_race`) took three values over five gate runs (A, B, A, B,
-  C). Each value gave all of about 600 `camcraft-app` units a new
-  directory. Third-party units did not change: their profile has no
-  incremental setting, and they stayed Fresh.
-- The agents that use that worktree ran gates with different env. One
-  worker restarted its gate with `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0`; the others used
-  the default (incremental on for workspace members). `CARGO_INCREMENTAL`
-  sets `profile.incremental`, which is part of the profile hash.
-- Nothing in `xtask/src` sets a profile, features, `--config` or rustflags
-  for a gate step. Inside one run, the per-crate `-p` builds (#2727) give
-  the lower crates one variant for each feature resolution. That set is the
-  same in each run, so a second run reuses it.

-catalog builds that already take the gate cache env) gets
-`CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0` and loses the caller's `CARGO_PROFILE_*` and
-`CARGO_BUILD_INCREMENTAL` variables (`xtask/src/unit_env.rs`). The gate
-prints the pin at its start, names each removed variable, and notes a set
-`RUSTFLAGS` / `CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS` / `CARGO_BUILD_RUSTFLAGS`. The
-summary prints the number of unit directories that the run added (0 on a
-second run of the same tree).

-so with incremental on the workspace crates never hit the shared cache.
-Incremental data also adds to the size of each unit, and disk is the
-defect here. The coordinator already set `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0` for all

-  sanitizer). The gate notes it instead.

-## #3169 - The gate removes superseded test-harness units at the end of each run
-
-**Cause.** Read in the shared build worktree `issue-917` on 2026-11-21 (read only):
-
-- One run does not give one target hundreds of hashes. The 634 `camcraft-app`
-  unit directories that were left after a sweep are 627 distinct targets: one
-  unit for each integration test binary (`crates/app/tests` has about 620
-  suites), plus the lib, the bins and the lib tests. Each test binary is its
-  own linked executable with its `.pdb`, about 100 MB, so one set is about
-  64 GB. Only 5 targets had a second variant, from a cargo call outside the
-  gate with another dependency feature resolution.
-- The growth is across trees and env. `camcraft-motion` had 747 units for 124
-  targets (six variants), `camcraft-post` 554 for 110, `camcraft-sim` 462 for
-  92. The variants differ in the profile hash (agents with other env before
-  #3154) or in the fingerprints of registry dependencies (other `serde_core`
-  feature sets). `Cargo.lock` and the manifests were the same at the heads
-  `8b4209215` and `cc04d7bcd`.
-- Cargo never removes a superseded variant. So each change of the env or of
-  a feature resolution adds a full set, about 60 GB for `camcraft-app`. The
-  count "629 to 4386" included these older sets.
-
-**Decided.** At the end of each gate run (green, red or void; never in a dry
-run), `xtask/src/unit_sweep.rs` removes a unit directory only when all of
-these are true:
-
-- it is under `target/debug/build` or `target/release/build` of the gate's
-  own root, and no `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`, `CARGO_BUILD_TARGET_DIR` or
-  `CARGO_BUILD_BUILD_DIR` points elsewhere;
-- its one target fingerprint is a test-harness target (`test-lib-`,
-  `test-integration-test-`, `test-bin-`);
-- another variant of the same target (profile, package, fingerprint name) was
-  written in this run, and this variant was written before the run started;
-- cargo's locks of each profile directory are free (the sweep holds them while
-  it deletes), and no other process names `<root>/target` in its command line
-  (another gate's xtask, a cargo or rustc there, a test executable);
-- no level of the path (`target`, the profile, `build`, the package, the unit,
-  `fingerprint`) is a symlink, a junction or another reparse point. A linked
-  profile directory or `target/` stops the whole sweep; a linked package or
-  unit is skipped. The unit is checked again just before its delete.
-
-The process check matches each form of `<root>/target`: the path as given,
-its absolute and clean form, and the canonical form (a subst drive, a
-junction, `/var` and `/private/var` on macOS). On Windows the match ignores
-case. A root form that cannot be resolved, a process list that cannot be read,
-or a cargo lock that cannot be probed counts as "unsure": nothing is removed.
-
-A failed delete is a warning line, never a gate failure. The summary
-prints the number of directories and the GB removed, or why the sweep did not
-run. `CAMCRAFT_GATE_SWEEP=off` (or `0`) turns it off.
-
-**Why at the end, and in any outcome.** A variant that this run wrote is the
-one that this tree uses. The superseded variant is used again only when the
-worktree goes back to a tree with the earlier resolution; then cargo builds
-those targets again (minutes) instead of keeping 60 GB. A red test does not
-make the new units wrong, so the outcome does not change the choice.
-
-**The lock of `cargo xtask` itself.** `cargo xtask` is `cargo run -p xtask`.
-Cargo holds the build lock of `target/debug` only while it compiles, and frees
-it before it starts the binary. The proof by reading: each gate step starts a
-cargo build into the same `target/debug` while `cargo xtask` is alive; if the
-outer cargo held the lock, every gate would wait for it without end. So the
-lock probe at the end of a run sees only other builds.
-
-**Why only test-harness units.** A test executable is built only when its
-own package is selected, and the gate selects one package for each step, so a
-target has one valid variant in a tree. A library can have two valid variants
-in one tree (for `-p geometry` and for `-p motion`); removing one costs a

-## #3184 - Post-merge gate: one independent run per merge
-
-**Decided.** `post-merge.yml` uses one concurrency group for each commit,
-`post-merge-${{ inputs.ref || github.sha }}`, with `cancel-in-progress:
-false`. Each push runs on a free `camcraft-post-merge` runner and always
-finishes. The `gate` job does not change. The `report` job has its own
-group, `post-merge-report` (`cancel-in-progress: false`), and checks out the
-full history (`fetch-depth: 0`). `.github/scripts/post-merge-report.sh`
-keeps the last reported commit in a hidden marker in the rolling issue body,
-`<!-- post-merge-last-sha: <sha> -->`. A run whose commit is a strict
-ancestor of that commit (`git merge-base --is-ancestor`, not the same
-commit) prints a notice and reports nothing.
-
-**Why.** With one group for `main`, a second push waited and a third push
-cancelled the waiting run. A red run then covered several merges, and the
-breaking merge needed a bisect (#3111). With one run for each commit, a red
-run names one commit. Runs can now finish out of order, so the report must
-not let an older green run close the issue of a newer red run.
-
-**Details chosen.**
-- The marker is read from the newest rolling issue, open or closed. A green
-  run with no open issue writes its commit into the closed issue's marker.
-  Without that, an older red run that finishes later would open a new issue
-  after a newer green run.
-- The same commit (a re-run) is not older than itself, and it reports.
-- If git cannot resolve the marker or this commit, the run reports as
-  before (fail open to a report, never to silence).
-- A new red issue carries the marker in its body. A red comment and a green
-  close write the marker into the issue body (the old marker line is
-  replaced).
-
-**Dropped.**
-- A repository variable or a separate state file for the last sha: the
-  issue asks for no new secrets or variables, and the rolling issue is
-  already the one shared state.
-- Comparing commit dates instead of ancestry: dates of merge commits are not
-  an order guarantee.
-
-**Known limit.** GitHub keeps at most one pending job in a concurrency
-group. If three report jobs wait at once, GitHub cancels the middle one.
-That report is lost; the next run on `main` reports the newer state. With
-two runners and a gate of about 20 min, three reports at once are rare.
-
-**Cost to change later.** Low. The marker is one line in the issue body;
-removing the guard returns the old behaviour.

-## #3211 - The wire gouge depth reads how far the wire stands inside the part
-
-**Decided.** The kerf law reads a signed clearance (`dist::entry`). When a
-move stands in the product, the reading is minus the distance from the
-move's deepest point to the product's boundary. The gouge depth is then the
-kerf reach plus that distance. Before, the clearance was 0 for such a move,
-so each gouge read the kerf offset alone (0.162 mm on a 2.8 mm entry).
-
-**Why.** The verify message names a depth and "the deepest reading at any
-height". An operator uses that number to decide what to change (the verify
-tolerance, the model, the path). A depth that is always the kerf offset
-hides how far the cut enters the part. The verdict stays the same: each
-move that gouged before still gouges, and the post stays blocked.
-
-**How the deepest point is found.** Split the move at each product boundary
-crossing, including the stock boundary for a die. Search every inside
-interval with endpoint bounds on its 1-Lipschitz boundary distance. Refine
-an interval while its bound can exceed the best reading by more than the
-move length divided by 1024. The reported depth underestimates the deepest
-entry by at most that amount, apart from floating-point roundoff. The
-reported point is inside the product. An excluded stock boundary can hold
-the supremum; the search approaches it from inside to the same tolerance.
-The two move ends are read exactly when they belong to the product.
-
-The former coarse walk and local refinement could miss a whole inside
-interval. Its stated error bound was false. The review's 100 mm move
-through the square at X=[50.5625, 52.5625] now reads a 1 mm entry. Global
-interval bounds replace that local search; another deeper interval cannot
-be discarded because its coarse samples are outside.
-
-**Dropped.**
-- An exact maximum through the medial axis of the section: much more code
-  for a number that only sizes a refused gouge.
-- A change to the threading and open-end laws: they need only "in or not
-  clear", and they say "at the point itself" for 0. They stay on the
-  unsigned `clearance`.
-- A change to which move the finding names: it stays the first move that
-  gouges at the first plane, with the deepest reading over all planes.
-
-**Cost to change later.** One function in `crates/sim/src/verify/wire/dist.rs`
-and its two callers.

-## #917 - kernel and geometry parity for the solidcore STEP path (PR B0)
-
-PR B0 holds the items of #917 that we can pin under the app. PR B (the

-
-### The coordinate snap (`camcraft_kernel::mesh_weld`)
-
-- **Decided.** Before the exact-position weld of the machining mesh, each
-  coordinate goes through one rule:
-  - The grid is 1e-3 mm (`SNAP_GRID_MM`). The window is 1e-9 mm
-    (`SNAP_WINDOW_MM`).
-  - `k = round(c / 1e-3)`, `g = k / 1000` (one IEEE 754 division).
-  - If `|c - g| <= 1e-9`, the coordinate becomes `g + 0.0`. Otherwise it
-    stays bit for bit. A coordinate that is not finite, or with
-    `|k| > 9e15`, stays.
-  - `+0.0` replaces `-0.0`. Equal inputs always give equal outputs.
-- **Degenerate facets.** A triangle whose corners snap or weld onto a
-  repeated vertex has no area. The weld drops it. The side count after
-  the weld (`sides`) then refuses the mesh with `NotWatertight` if the
-  drop opened a hole. No facet is moved past the window to close a gap.
-- **Why.** The evaluator gives 20.000000000000004 for a face at Z 20. The
-  app's flat-level and floor logic compares levels exactly, so a level
-  read off the mesh by one ulp gives a wrong floor. The window is far under
-  any machining tolerance (the smallest tolerance is a millionth of the
-  body). A vertex moves at most one window in each axis, sqrt(3) x 1e-9
-  = 1.73e-9 mm (`SNAP_MOVE_MM`), so the measured deviation stays true to
-  1.73e-9 mm. The mesher adds `SNAP_MOVE_MM` to the measured deviation
-  before it compares it with the tolerance, so the judged figure holds
-  for the snapped mesh too (review of #2843).
-- **Dropped.** A snap to the 1e-6 grid (it would move true model values
-  such as 12.5000004). A relative window (a large part would move more).
-  A snap after the weld (two near copies of one vertex then weld
-  differently).
-- **Pinned by** `the_snap_takes_the_last_bit_noise_off_a_grid_value`,
-  `a_coordinate_outside_the_window_is_never_moved` (12.5 +/- 1e-6 stays)
-  and `the_bore_mesh_stands_on_its_exact_levels`.

-  group of triangles joined side to side, `mesh_weld::shells`) with a

-### A breaking edge or swept spline is refused by name (`step_curve_guard`)

-- **Decided.** Before the topology read, the reader scans each B-spline
-  curve that an `EDGE_CURVE` (through `SURFACE_CURVE`, `SEAM_CURVE`,
-  `INTERSECTION_CURVE`) or a swept surface
-  (`SURFACE_OF_LINEAR_EXTRUSION`, `SURFACE_OF_REVOLUTION`) uses. It refuses
